name: Central Semitic
region: The Levant, Syria and northern Arabia
defining_innovation: A new imperfective, yaqtulu, replaced the older yiqattal type: Arabic yaktubu and Hebrew yikhtov 'he writes', against Ge'ez yəqättəl, which keeps the old pattern.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body:
Central Semitic groups Arabic with the Northwest Semitic languages: Hebrew, Phoenician, Aramaic and Ugaritic. Robert Hetzron set it out in the 1970s, and it has since become the standard view, with John Huehnergard as its main defender. The key evidence is in the verb. The present-future form of the old type, still seen in Akkadian *iparras* and Ge'ez *yəqättəl*, was replaced by a new form built on the old past-tense prefix: Arabic *yaktubu*, Hebrew *yikhtov*.

This was a change of view. For a long time Arabic was classed with the South Semitic languages of Arabia and Ethiopia, which share with it the 'broken plurals' (Arabic *kitāb* 'book', plural *kutub*). That older grouping appears here as a dotted arc between Arabic and Ethiosemitic.

chapters.title: Arabic and Hebrew Side by Side
chapters.body:
Because Arabic and Hebrew are both well documented and closely enough related, they are the pair most often used to show what Central Semitic shares, and where its two halves went separate ways.

The common ground is easy to see. Both form the past with suffixes and the present-future with prefixes built on the same stem: Arabic *kataba* 'he wrote', *yaktubu* 'he writes'; Hebrew *kātav*, *yikhtōv*. Both have a definite article that the older Semitic languages lacked, though they built it differently: Arabic prefixes *al-* (*al-bayt* 'the house'), Hebrew *ha-* with doubling of the next consonant (*ha-bbayit*). Aramaic went its own way again, marking definiteness with a suffix *-ā* (*baytā*). The article probably arose separately in each line after they parted, a sign that Proto-Central Semitic had none.

The differences are in the sounds and the plurals. Arabic kept almost the full Proto-Semitic set of consonants, including `*ṯ` and `*ḏ`, which Hebrew merged with *š* and *z*. Hebrew and Aramaic, on the other hand, lost the case endings that Classical Arabic preserves (*-u*, *-i*, *-a*), and they rarely use Arabic's internal 'broken' plurals, preferring suffixes: Hebrew *sūs* 'horse', *sūsīm* 'horses'.

speakers.note: Arabic accounts for nearly all of them; Hebrew adds about 5 million and Neo-Aramaic a few hundred thousand.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig, eds. 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.

turning_points.title: Arabic and Northwest Semitic part
turning_points.description: The ancestors of Arabic in northern Arabia and of the Northwest Semitic languages in the Levant and Syria diverge. The date is inferred rather than documented: Arabic is not written until the first millennium BCE.

sources.citation: Huehnergard, John & Aaron D. Rubin. 2011. Phyla and waves: Models of classification of the Semitic languages. In The Semitic Languages: An International Handbook, ed. Stefan Weninger. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

contested_classifications.proposed_grouping: Arabic as South Semitic: Arabic belongs with the Ethiopian and South Arabian languages rather than with Hebrew and Aramaic
contested_classifications.evidence_for: Arabic shares 'broken' internal plurals with Ethiosemitic and South Arabian (*kitāb* 'book' → *kutub*), and the peoples were neighbours across Arabia. This was the standard classification in 19th- and early 20th-century handbooks.
contested_classifications.evidence_against: Broken plurals are probably an old Semitic feature that the Northwest Semitic languages mostly lost, so sharing them proves nothing. Arabic shares with Northwest Semitic the new imperfective *yaqtulu* and other innovations. Following Hetzron and Huehnergard, Arabic is now generally placed in Central Semitic.

sources.citation: Hetzron, Robert. 1976. Two principles of genetic reconstruction. Lingua 38.
